title: Reality as Ideological Construct: A Reading of Five Novels by Philip K. Dick
author: Peter Fitting
card_summary: A Marxist-informed scholarly article from Science Fiction Studies (Vol. 10, No. 2, July 1983) reading five Dick novels through the lens of ideology and constructed reality. Fitting examines how Dick's fictional realities expose the ideological construction of consensus reality. 19 pages.
page_summary:
Reality as Ideological Construct: A Reading of Five Novels by Philip K. Dick is Peter Fitting's early Marxist intervention into PKD criticism and one of the foundational Science Fiction Studies essays on Dick. Published in July 1983, the article treats ideology not as a vague atmosphere but as a lived structure that organizes how Dick's characters perceive reality, themselves, and the social order. Fitting reads five novels - The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch, Ubik, A Maze of Death, Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, and Now Wait for Last Year - as different formal experiments in exposing that structure.

The article's central move is to refuse the idea that Dick's novels are simply metaphysical puzzles or private visionary documents. Instead, Fitting argues that their unstable worlds reveal the constructedness of bourgeois reality itself. That stance places the essay squarely in the Suvin/Althusser lineage of science-fiction criticism: Dick matters here because his fiction helps make ideology visible. The article is especially important because it helped establish Ubik as a canonical object of serious academic reading while also showing that Dick's recurring reality-breakdowns can be analyzed politically rather than only biographically or theologically.

In the later PKD literature, this essay becomes a reference point against which postmodern, biographical, and religious-studies readings define themselves. Its limitations are also part of its significance: Fitting's frame is deliberately demystifying, so it leaves less room for the visionary and mystical registers that later scholars, especially Palmer, McKee, and Kripal, would reopen. Even so, it remains one of the clearest early statements of the claim that Dick's fiction is not just about false worlds but about the social production of reality itself.
